title: 25 Years Since the Anthrax Attacks: Where Are We Now?
gist: A CSIS panel marking 25 years since the 2001 anthrax letters argues US biodefense architecture (ASPR, PAHPA, BioShield, Select Agent Program, CDC lab networks) improved materially, but warns that PAHPA lapsed without COVID lessons, AI-designed pathogens will erode attribution, and funding decays when no incident keeps Congress afraid.

insights.claim: Former Senator Richard Burr warned that AI-designed or AI-engineered pathogens may lack the familiar DNA signatures investigators rely on, making attribution of a biological attack much harder.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Weaker attribution undermines deterrence and raises tail risk premia for biothreat events.
insights.quote: we’re headed into a period where attribution is going to be much more difficult, with AI-designed pathogens that really don’t – they don’t contain the DNA that we are accustomed to looking at
insights.locator: Richard Burr: Well, let me also

insights.claim: Twenty-five years after the 2001 anthrax letters, there is still no agreed-upon explanation of who carried out the attacks; the US government settled a multimillion-dollar claim with one researcher it had publicly accused and later retracted.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Illustrates that even large domestic investigations can fail to attribute bio attacks, a structural deterrence gap.
insights.quote: It’s also worth noting that we still don’t have an agreed-upon explanation for who did this.
insights.locator: Paul Friedrichs: Thank you, Sophia

insights.claim: The US administration's compliance report states that both Russia and North Korea maintain bioweapons programs, and a suspected plague-related death at a Russian lab was in the news in October 2026.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: State bioweapons programs keep biodefense spending a persistent national-security line item.
insights.quote: This administration has published their compliance report, which highlights that both Russia and North Korea have bioweapons programs.
insights.locator: Paul Friedrichs: Thank you, Sophia

insights.claim: Paul Friedrichs argued there is an explosion of new high-containment research labs globally without a matching supply of experienced staff or regulators, alongside more countries and nonstate actors considering bioweapons.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Lab proliferation outpacing oversight raises accident and misuse risk, supporting demand for biosecurity and surveillance tools.
insights.quote: there’s no profusion of people with 20 years’ experience to work in them, nor is there a profusion of regulators and people to provide oversight to mitigate risk
insights.locator: Dr. Friedrichs: Well, the reality is

themes.theme: Legislative architecture and the PAHPA lapse

insights.claim: The Pandemic and All Hazards Preparedness Act (PAHPA) has not been reauthorized, so lessons from COVID and recent technology advances are not incorporated into the statutory biodefense architecture.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Reauthorization is a key legislative catalyst for funding flows to countermeasure and biosurveillance contractors.
insights.quote: We haven’t reauthorized PAHPA, which was the – which was the architecture.
insights.locator: Senator Burr: Well, this is

insights.claim: Burr said Congress typically appropriates for biodefense only after a frightening incident, and that long quiet periods let appropriators cut funding, eroding capabilities.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Biodefense budgets are event-driven and cyclical, making vendor revenue lumpy and incident-dependent.
insights.quote: it takes Congress having some type of fear of something for them to actually appropriate and to enforce the right behaviors
insights.locator: Richard Burr: Well, let me also

insights.claim: Burr argued bureaucratic stovepiping persists because power in Washington is measured by budget size, so agencies resist sharing missions or money.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Interagency fragmentation slows procurement of integrated data and surveillance platforms.
insights.quote: it’s simply because the power in Washington is determined by the size of a budget
insights.locator: Senator Burr: Well, Stu danced around

insights.claim: The original legislation envisioned the US vice president in the role that became HHS's Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response (ASPR), but Vice President Cheney rejected it, so ASPR was created inside HHS.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Explains why pandemic command sits at agency level rather than in the White House.
insights.locator: Senator Burr: Yeah, because it actually

insights.claim: Burr predicted that regardless of the current administration's actions in its last two years, the next administration will reinstate the power of the White House Office of Pandemic Preparedness and Response (OPPR).
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Signals likely policy swing toward centralized pandemic coordination after 2028.
insights.quote: regardless of what this administration does in its last two years, the next administration will reinstate the power of that component too
insights.locator: Senator Burr: Listen, it was a natural

insights.claim: Stewart Simonson described Project BioShield as a $5 billion over five years attempt to create a market for biodefense countermeasures that lacked commercial demand, calling it deeply flawed but improved upon by BARDA and PAHPA.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Government is the sole buyer for many countermeasures; program design dictates sector economics.
insights.quote: It was 5 billion (dollars) over five years.
insights.locator: Mr. Simonson: So BioShield was

insights.claim: The US stockpile now holds three anthrax therapies (two monoclonal antibodies and anthrax immunoglobulin), but still relies on a 1970s-era anthrax vaccine after a recombinant protective antigen vaccine never reached trials.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Points to an unmet next-generation vaccine need and incumbent-protected procurement.
insights.quote: Today we have three therapies, I believe, in the stockpile.
insights.locator: Mr. Simonson: That’s true.

insights.claim: Simonson said the next-generation anthrax vaccine effort failed partly because the incumbent licensed vaccine maker lobbied Congress once the rival product approached licensure.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Incumbent biodefense suppliers can use political channels to protect sole-source contracts.
insights.quote: what they were not satisfied with at HHS they litigated on Capitol Hill
insights.locator: Mr. Simonson: That’s true.

insights.claim: Burr argued that because countermeasure markets are poorly defined, capital for them can come only from government, and warned that AI regulation blocking IPOs would strand capital that historically funded socially beneficial R&D.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Links AI capital markets and IPO windows to biodefense R&D funding.
insights.quote: the attraction of capital can only happen from government. It can never happen from the private sector
insights.locator: Senator Burr: And, Paul, let me say

insights.claim: Burr flagged COVID-driven vaccine skepticism and a regional measles outbreak that could become national as the most alarming current issue Congress should address in reauthorization.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Vaccine hesitancy weighs on vaccine demand and raises outbreak risk.
insights.quote: COVID created a skepticism about vaccines. And we’re fighting a measles outbreak that’s very regional, but could be national at any point
insights.locator: Senator Burr: And, Paul, let me say

insights.claim: Friedrichs noted that every drug and mask in the US is made by private companies and credited COVID vaccine speed to academia-regulator-industry partnership.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Preparedness policy depends on industry partners, favoring firms with government-partnership capacity.
insights.quote: there are exactly zero drugs in the United States that are not made by a pharmaceutical company
insights.locator: Dr. Friedrichs: Well, the reality is

insights.claim: CDC's Biothreat Radar, which aims to integrate wastewater, traveler genomic and other surveillance streams, has been authorized but is not yet fully funded.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Appropriation would open contracts for data integration and genomic surveillance vendors.
insights.quote: I think it is – it’s still yet to be fully funded.
insights.locator: Dr. Kuhnert: Sure.

insights.claim: Friedrichs said companies learned from COVID that they need outbreak early warning and are now paying vendors for it, some of whom go beyond what Biothreat Radar offers.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A private commercial market for outbreak intelligence is emerging independent of federal budgets.
insights.quote: they are paying vendors to give them early warning that they feel comfortable with
insights.locator: Dr. Friedrichs: And the one slight caveat

insights.claim: Friedrichs cited that 70 percent of human outbreaks start in other species and called for merging animal, plant, human and intelligence data, plus social media signals, to detect outbreaks earlier.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Supports One Health data aggregation and AI analytics as a growth area.
insights.quote: We know that 70 percent of human outbreaks start in other species.
insights.locator: Dr. Friedrichs: Well, and so I will say

insights.claim: CDC's Wendi Kuhnert said environmental surface testing for anthrax was a gap in 2001 and remains one today, while ARPA-H's BREATHE program is developing a successor to BioWatch.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Environmental detection remains an unsolved procurement need.
insights.quote: the environmental testing, the ability to screen environmental surfaces, I think that – you know, that existed then, and, unfortunately, I think it still exists now
insights.locator: Wendi Kuhnert: OK, I’ll try

insights.claim: Kuhnert said CDC's surge diagnostic contracts with private companies, awarded under Mandy Cohen, were used for Zika and flu, though CDC is still learning how to write requirements for them.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Pre-negotiated surge testing capacity is a recurring revenue channel for diagnostics firms.
insights.locator: Dr. Kuhnert: No, but I’m aware

insights.claim: Panelists agreed the Federal Select Agent Program, widely emulated abroad, assumes biology is static and has not been updated for synthetic biology and AI, risking it losing pace with engineered organisms.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Expect regulatory updates extending to AI-bio tool developers, affecting biotech and AI firms.
insights.quote: with synthetic biology and with superintelligence, we will lose pace with that
insights.locator: Dr. Kuhnert: I think that’s a really

insights.claim: Friedrichs suggested future legislation should regulate not just users of AI-bio tools but the companies that develop them, analogous to FDA oversight of equipment.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: AI model developers may face biosecurity compliance obligations.
insights.locator: Dr. Friedrichs: And I and I’ll echo

insights.claim: An audience member who worked at Fort Detrick argued biosecurity should shift from list-based to risk-based regulation with personnel reliability as its core.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Points toward broader, risk-based oversight scope.
insights.locator: Audience Question: Howdy.

insights.claim: Burr said that with a White House near the end of its term and polarized party fringes, biodefense champions must be built in the middle of both parties, with leadership tacitly endorsing action.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Bipartisan biodefense legislation faces a narrow path near term.
insights.locator: Senator Burr: Yeah. Thanks.

insights.claim: Friedrichs said Congress hears inconsistent messaging from biodefense advocates and that speaking with one voice would substantially improve legislative outcomes.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Fragmented advocacy contributes to underfunding.
